data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a methodological decision to act on the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, thereby maximizing the content of potential error and aligning with the regulative idea of truth (verisimilitude) without claiming probabilistic justification.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If corroboration reports are shown to logically entail a probability increase for future performance, the non-inductive defense collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's concept of verisimilitude is proven formally incoherent (as per Tich\u00fd/Miller) such that it cannot guide preference even as a regulative ideal.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the distinction between 'psychological expectation' and 'rational methodological choice' is demonstrated to be untenable in practical action scenarios.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'Critical Preferential Selection': agents treat corroboration reports not as evidence of probability, but as a status marker indicating which theory currently offers the best opportunity for learning (highest falsifiability) and closest approximation to truth, given that all other competitors have been eliminated. The preference is a rational volitional act aligned with the aim of science, distinct from an inductive expectation of nature's uniformity.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
